title: MYCIN thesis milestone
summary: Edward H. Shortliffe's Stanford thesis documented MYCIN as a rule-based computer program designed to advise physicians regarding antimicrobial therapy selection. Stanford's computer-science report bibliography lists the thesis in October 1974 and describes MYCIN's consultation, explanation, and rule-acquisition components.
significance: A documented 1974 research milestone for a rule-based medical consultation system, represented as a thesis/documentation event rather than as an asserted invention or system-birth date.

verification.note: Stanford's bibliography of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory reports identifies Edward H. Shortliffe's thesis 'MYCIN: A Rule-Based Computer Program for Advising Physicians Regarding Antimicrobial Therapy Selection' as an October 1974 Ph.D. thesis and describes MYCIN as a rule-based problem-solving system for therapy selection in bacterial infections, including consultation, explanation, and rule-acquisition components. A later Stanford presentation by Shortliffe identifies the MYCIN Project as spanning 1972-1979. This candidate intentionally uses year precision and represents the documented thesis milestone only. It does not convert October 1974 into MYCIN's invention, project-start, deployment, or system-birth date; does not infer development geography beyond Stanford's role as the thesis institution; and adds no ancestry, influence, causality, universal-priority claim, or relationship edge.

sources.title: Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory report bibliography (AIM-251 / CS-465)

candidateMeta.admissionReason: Primary Stanford institutional material supports the thesis identity, author, 1974 chronology, MYCIN name, rule-based medical-consultation scope, and system-component description. The record deliberately preserves this as a thesis/documentation milestone and avoids unsupported system-birth, invention, deployment, geography, ancestry, influence, or causality claims.
